quizzes.title: How Does God Save? A Which View Am I Quiz
quizzes.intro: These questions ask how you currently think about the way God rescues and keeps a person. Answer with your honest instinct rather than the answer you think you are supposed to give.
quizzes.disclaimer: This is a starting point for self-understanding, not a verdict on where you must land. A quiz cannot weigh a doctrine, and faithful Christians who love the same Scriptures have held each of these positions with care.

questions.q: When you read that someone came to faith, what feels most true to you about how it happened?

options.label: God first changed the heart so that the person was able to believe and gladly did
God drew near and gave grace, and the person was enabled to either receive or resist it
God made the offer plain, and the person was free to trust the message as it stood

questions.q: How do you understand who Christ died for?

options.label: He died with particular purpose to secure the salvation of those given to him
He died for everyone, and that death becomes effective when a person believes
He died for every person without exception, and the gift stands ready for all

questions.q: What do you make of the word election in Scripture?

options.label: God chose specific people for salvation according to his own purpose
God chose those he foreknew would respond to his grace with faith
Election speaks of God's plan and people more than the picking of individuals to save

questions.q: Can a person finally turn away and lose salvation?

options.label: No, those God truly saves he will surely keep to the end
Yes, a believer can abandon the faith and forfeit the gift
The one who is saved is secure, though I hold that lightly and want to honor the warnings too

questions.q: How do you picture the human will after the fall?

options.label: So bound by sin that no one seeks God until grace renews the will
Unable on its own, yet freed to respond once God's grace goes before
Damaged by sin yet still able to hear the gospel and trust it when it comes

questions.q: When grace comes to a heart God intends to save, what happens?

options.label: It surely accomplishes its purpose and the person comes willingly
It enables a real response, and the person may still say no
It persuades without overriding, and the person remains free to refuse

questions.q: Why does one person believe and another does not?

options.label: Because God in mercy granted faith to the one and not the other
Because both were given grace and one cooperated while the other resisted
Because the gospel was offered to both and one trusted it while the other declined

questions.q: Which sentence sits most comfortably with you?

options.label: Salvation is God's work from beginning to end, and I rest in that
Salvation is God's gift that asks for a free and ongoing yes
Salvation is offered to all, and God leaves the response genuinely open

results.name: Leaning Reformed (Calvinist)
results.blurb: You tend to see salvation as God's sovereign work, with grace that renews the heart before a person can believe and keeps that person to the end. This view treasures the security of resting in what God alone accomplishes. Many thoughtful believers find here a deep comfort that the whole of their rescue is held in stronger hands than their own.

results.name: Leaning Arminian
results.blurb: You tend to see salvation as God's grace given to all, with a genuine human response that God enables but does not force. This view guards the reality of love freely returned and the seriousness of Scripture's warnings. Many faithful Christians have found here a way to hold both God's initiative and human responsibility together.

results.name: Leaning Provisionist
results.blurb: You tend to see the cross as a provision made for every person, with the gospel offered plainly and the response left truly free. This view stresses that God desires all to be saved and withholds the gift from no one. Many believers are drawn here by the wide and open invitation they read across the pages of Scripture.

quizzes.title: Baptism and the Church: A Which View Am I Quiz
quizzes.intro: These questions ask how you currently think about baptism, the gathered church, and the way grace meets us in both. Answer with the view that feels most natural to you right now.
quizzes.disclaimer: This is a starting point for self-understanding, not a verdict on which church is right. A short quiz cannot settle questions the church has weighed for centuries, and sincere believers have followed each of these paths with conviction and love.

questions.q: Who do you believe is a fitting candidate for baptism?

options.label: Believers and the infants of the faithful, received into the life of grace
Believers and their children, brought under the sign of the covenant
Those who profess personal faith for themselves

questions.q: What is happening in the act of baptism itself?

options.label: God truly conveys grace through the sign, joining the person to Christ
God seals his covenant promise, and faith lays hold of what it signifies
The believer publicly testifies to a faith already received

questions.q: How do you think of the Lord's Supper?

options.label: Christ is truly present and given to us in the bread and the cup
Christ is present by his Spirit to feed those who come in faith
The bread and cup call us to remember Christ's death with thankful hearts

questions.q: How should the church be led and ordered?

options.label: Through bishops and an ordered ministry handed down across the ages
Through elders gathered in connected councils that share oversight
Through the local congregation governing its own life under Christ

questions.q: What makes a person a member of the church?

options.label: Incorporation through the sacraments into the one historic body
Belonging to the covenant community marked out by its sign
A personal profession of faith joined to a local body of believers

questions.q: How do you weigh church tradition alongside Scripture?

options.label: Scripture and the living tradition of the church belong together
Scripture rules, and the historic confessions guide our reading of it
Scripture stands as the final word, read freshly by each gathered church

questions.q: When a child is raised in the church, how do you see that child?

options.label: Already brought into grace through the sacrament of baptism
Already a member of the covenant, awaiting a personal embrace of faith
Loved and nurtured, awaiting their own faith and baptism in time

questions.q: Which sentence rings most true to you?

options.label: Grace meets us through the appointed signs of the visible church
God works through covenant signs that promise and seal his grace
The church is a fellowship of those who have personally trusted Christ

results.name: Leaning Catholic and Sacramental
results.blurb: You tend to see grace as truly given through the sacraments and the ordered life of the historic church. This view holds Scripture and the living tradition closely together and treasures the visible continuity of the body across the centuries. Many believers find here a sense of being received into something far older and larger than themselves.

results.name: Leaning Reformed and Presbyterian
results.blurb: You tend to see baptism as a covenant sign that seals God's promise to believers and their children, with the church led by elders in connected councils. This view honors the historic confessions while holding Scripture as the rule. Many Christians value the way it joins the children of the faithful to the covenant community.

results.name: Leaning Baptist and Free Church
results.blurb: You tend to see baptism as the public testimony of those who personally profess faith, with each congregation ordering its own life under Christ. This view treasures the clarity of believer's baptism and the final authority of Scripture. Many find here a fellowship gathered around shared and chosen faith.

quizzes.title: The End Times and the Millennium: A Which View Am I Quiz
quizzes.intro: These questions ask how you currently picture Christ's return, the thousand years of Revelation, and the shape of history's end. Answer with the instinct you hold today.
quizzes.disclaimer: This is a starting point for self-understanding, not a verdict on how the end will come. Godly readers of the same prophecies have differed here for a very long time, and humility belongs to all of us when we speak of what is still to come.

questions.q: How do you read the thousand years in Revelation chapter twenty?

options.label: As a picture of Christ's present reign between his first and second coming
As an age of growing gospel influence before Christ returns
As a real future age that begins when Christ comes back
As a future earthly kingdom centered on God's promises to Israel

questions.q: What do you expect history to look like before Christ returns?

options.label: A mingling of growth and trouble until the very end
A gradual ripening as the gospel spreads and bears fruit across the world
Increasing difficulty for the church before Christ breaks in
A rising tribulation tied to God's unfolding plan for Israel and the nations

questions.q: When does the millennium begin in relation to Christ's return?

options.label: There is no separate earthly thousand years, the reign is now
Christ returns after the long age of gospel triumph
Christ returns first, and then the thousand years follow
Christ returns to establish the thousand year kingdom on earth

questions.q: How do you understand the place of Israel in prophecy?

options.label: The promises find their fullness in Christ and his whole people
The promises advance as the gospel gathers all nations over time
Israel and the church share in one people, united in Christ
God keeps distinct promises to Israel that await a future fulfillment

questions.q: How do you read the prophetic symbols and numbers of Revelation?

options.label: Largely as symbols picturing the whole age of the church
As pointing to the steady advance of Christ's kingdom in history
As real future events, read with care for their symbolic weight
As a fairly literal map of events still to unfold in order

questions.q: What is your sense of the church's mission and its outcome in history?

options.label: Faithful witness amid both harvest and hardship until Christ comes
A hopeful work that will see the nations widely turn to Christ
Steadfast endurance through trial as we await his appearing
Urgent witness as God's program moves toward its appointed seasons

questions.q: When you hear the word rapture, what comes to mind?

options.label: Believers meeting the returning Lord at the single great coming
The gathering of the saints when Christ comes after the age of growth
The church caught up to the Lord as he returns in glory
A distinct catching away of the church before a coming tribulation

questions.q: Which sentence captures your hope for the end?

options.label: Christ reigns now and will return to make all things new
The gospel will fill the earth before Christ comes in glory
Christ will return, then reign, then bring the final renewal
Christ will gather his church, then keep his promises to Israel in a coming kingdom

results.name: Leaning Amillennial
results.blurb: You tend to read the thousand years as a picture of Christ's present reign rather than a separate earthly age, with one return that renews all things. This view holds together the harvest and the hardship of the church's life until the end. Many believers find here a steady hope rooted in a Lord who already reigns.

results.name: Leaning Postmillennial
results.blurb: You tend to expect the gospel to spread and bear wide fruit through history before Christ returns in glory. This view carries a strong hope that the nations will largely come to faith over time. Many Christians are drawn here by its confidence in the reach of Christ's kingdom.

results.name: Leaning Historic Premillennial
results.blurb: You tend to expect Christ to return and then reign for a real future age, with the church enduring trial until he appears. This view reads Israel and the church as one people united in Christ. Many believers value its long roots in the early church and its blend of realism and hope.

results.name: Leaning Dispensational
results.blurb: You tend to expect a future earthly kingdom in which God keeps distinct promises to Israel, often with a catching away of the church before a coming tribulation. This view reads prophecy fairly directly and watches history move through appointed seasons. Many find here a strong sense of God's faithfulness to every word he has spoken.

quizzes.title: Genesis and Origins: A Which View Am I Quiz
quizzes.intro: These questions ask how you currently read Genesis 1 and 2 and how you relate the text to the sciences. Answer with your honest instinct, not the answer you think a good Christian is supposed to give.
quizzes.disclaimer: This is a starting point for self-understanding, not a verdict on how God made the world. This is third-order ground, and faithful Christians who confess the same Creator have held each of these readings with a clear conscience.

questions.q: When you read the six days of Genesis 1, what do you take them to be?

options.label: Six ordinary days, meant as plainly as the text reads
Six real and sequential creative periods, each far longer than a day
A true telling of who created and why, not a timetable of how long
A literary frame arranged by theme, teaching order and authority rather than chronology

questions.q: How old do you take the earth to be?

options.label: Thousands of years, as the genealogies suggest when read straightforwardly
Ancient, as the rocks and starlight indicate, and Genesis allows exactly that
Ancient, and the sciences that date it are describing God's long handiwork
The text does not say, because Genesis was never answering that question

questions.q: What do you make of animal death before Adam?

options.label: There was none. Death of every kind entered the world through the fall
Animals died in the long ages before Adam, and Scripture's concern is human death
Death was part of the natural process God used, and the fall brought humanity's guilt and estrangement
Genesis 1 is not addressing the biology of death, so I hold that question loosely

questions.q: Who were Adam and Eve?

options.label: The first two humans, specially formed on the sixth day, ancestors of us all
Real people specially created by God, however long ago the rest took
Real representatives God appointed from among early humanity, or a truth told through them, with Christians differing
The truly fallen first covenant pair, with the shape of the days telling us nothing about the calendar of their making

questions.q: When mainstream science and your reading of Genesis conflict, what is your first instinct?

options.label: Scripture's plain sense stands, and the scientific consensus should be re-examined
Recheck the interpretation, since God's word and God's world cannot finally disagree
Trust the well-tested science and ask what the text was actually written to teach
Ask whether the text was ever speaking to that question at all

questions.q: What is Genesis 1 chiefly for?

options.label: A true record of how and when God made everything, the foundation of all history
A true account of the order of God's creative work, told so every age can read it
A declaration of the one Creator against the idols, teaching who and why rather than how
A portrait of God ordering his house, built with the care of a poem and the weight of a creed

questions.q: What role should the sciences play in reading Genesis?

options.label: They can illustrate the text, but they never overrule its plain sense
They are God-given light on the age and scale of his works, read alongside the text
They describe the very process God used, so they belong in the conversation from the start
They answer their own questions, and Genesis answers different ones, so neither needs to referee the other

questions.q: Which sentence sits closest to your instinct?

options.label: I would rather trust the plain reading than adjust it to the spirit of the age
The God of the Bible is the God of the rocks and the starlight, and they tell one story across long ages
Evolution is not a rival creator, only a tool in the Creator's hand
Genesis tells me whose world this is, and leaves the clock to him

results.name: Leaning Young-Earth Creationism
results.blurb: You tend to read Genesis 1 as a plain account of six ordinary days a few thousand years ago, with death entering through Adam's sin. This view treasures the straightforward sense of Scripture and refuses to let any outside authority stand over the text. Many believers value its courage and its consistency, holding the plain reading whatever it costs.

results.name: Leaning Old-Earth Creation
results.blurb: You tend to read the days of Genesis as long, real, sequential periods, taking the antiquity of the earth as God's own testimony in the rocks and stars. This view holds Scripture and the sciences together as two books of one Author. Many Christians find here a way to honor both the text and the telescope without forcing either.

results.name: Leaning Evolutionary Creation
results.blurb: You tend to see evolution as the means God used to create, with Genesis teaching who made the world and why rather than the biological mechanism. This view keeps the Creator's sovereignty over the whole process and reads Genesis 1 against the idols of the ancient world. Many believers in the sciences have found here a faith that does not ask them to leave their work at the door.

results.name: Leaning the Framework View
results.blurb: You tend to read Genesis 1 as a carefully built literary account, arranged by theme to display God's ordering of creation, without intending to date the earth or clock the days. This view takes the text's artistry seriously as part of its inspiration. Many find here a reading that lets Genesis say exactly what it says without conscripting it into modern debates.

quizzes.title: What Happens at the Table? A Which View Am I Quiz
quizzes.intro: These questions ask what you currently believe happens at the Lord's Supper, in the bread, in the cup, and in you. Answer with your honest instinct, whatever your church's official position.
quizzes.disclaimer: This is a starting point for self-understanding, not a ruling on the deepest mystery Christians share. The four historic views were each held by believers willing to die for Christ, and the doctrine page states every one of them at full strength.

questions.q: When the bread is consecrated at the Table, what happens to it?

options.label: It truly becomes the body of Christ, though every appearance of bread remains
It remains bread, and Christ's true body is present in, with, and under it
It remains bread, and by the Spirit it becomes the instrument through which Christ feeds his people
It remains bread, set apart as a sign to proclaim the Lord's death until he comes

questions.q: How is Christ present at the Supper?

options.label: In his whole substance, body and blood, under the appearances of bread and wine
Bodily and truly, joined to the bread and wine by his own word of promise
Truly but spiritually, as the Spirit lifts believers to feed on the ascended Christ by faith
As he is present wherever his people gather in his name, remembered and proclaimed

questions.q: What does a person without faith receive if they eat?

options.label: The body of Christ itself, though to their harm rather than their blessing
The true body and blood, received by mouth, but to judgment rather than benefit
Bread and wine only, since Christ is received by faith or not at all
Bread and wine, and the danger of treating lightly what the church holds sacred

questions.q: When Jesus said, this is my body, how do you hear it?

options.label: Exactly as spoken, trusting his word over the evidence of the senses
As a plain promise that where this bread is given, there his body is given
As covenant language, the sign so joined to the reality that it bears the reality's name
As he meant the vine and the door, a living figure that carries his meaning

questions.q: What is the Supper chiefly doing for you?

options.label: Feeding me with Christ himself, the sacrifice of the cross made present to his church
Placing into my hands the forgiveness his death won, as certain as taste
Nourishing my union with Christ, sealing the promise the way bread strengthens the body
Calling me back to the cross with thanksgiving, binding me to my Lord and his people

questions.q: How do you read John 6, eating the flesh of the Son of Man?

options.label: As pointing squarely to the Eucharist, where his flesh is true food indeed
As fulfilled wherever his true body is given with the bread for believers to eat
As the feeding of faith on Christ, which the Supper then pictures and applies
As a vivid figure for trusting him, spoken before the Supper ever existed

questions.q: Why has the church guarded the Table so carefully?

options.label: Because the Lord himself is there, and what is holy must be treated as holy
Because his body and blood are truly handled there, and the promise is not to be trifled with
Because the sign and seal of the covenant belongs to those inside the covenant
Because the memorial of his death deserves clean hands and an examined heart

questions.q: Which sentence rings truest to you?

options.label: The Eucharist is the source and summit of the church's whole life
At the altar the gospel becomes touchable, given and shed for you
At the Table, heaven does not come down so much as faith is lifted up
The bread announces him until he comes, and the announcing is the glory of it

results.name: Leaning Transubstantiation
results.blurb: You tend to believe the bread and wine become, in their whole substance, the body and blood of Christ, while their appearances remain. This is the Roman Catholic confession, resting on the plain force of the words of institution and the church's unbroken practice of adoration. Many find here the most concrete possible assurance that Christ gives himself to his people.

results.name: Leaning the Lutheran View
results.blurb: You tend to believe Christ's true body and blood are present in, with, and under the bread and wine, received by all who eat, because his word says so. This view refuses both philosophy's explanations and metaphor's escape, taking the promise at face value. Many treasure the certainty it gives, forgiveness placed into the hand.

results.name: Leaning the Reformed View
results.blurb: You tend to believe Christ is truly given and truly received at the Table, not by his body descending into bread, but by the Spirit lifting believers to feed on the whole, ascended Christ through faith. This view keeps the Supper a real means of grace while honoring the ascension. Many find here both reverence and warmth, a true feeding without a physical mechanism.

results.name: Leaning Memorialism
results.blurb: You tend to see the Supper as a covenant meal of remembrance, proclamation, and pledged allegiance, with Christ present as he is always present among his gathered people. This view guards the once-for-all completeness of the cross and the simplicity of the meal Jesus gave. Many value how it keeps the sign pointing away from itself to the finished work.

quizzes.title: Do the Miraculous Gifts Continue? A Which View Am I Quiz
quizzes.intro: These questions ask what you currently believe about prophecy, tongues, and healing in the church today. Answer from your convictions as they stand, not from your best or worst experience of them.
quizzes.disclaimer: This is a starting point for self-understanding, not a measure of anyone's experience of the Spirit. Believers filled with love for the same Lord have landed in each of these places, and the doctrine page gives every position its strongest case.

questions.q: What were the miraculous gifts chiefly for?

options.label: To authenticate the apostles and the arriving word of God, a task now complete
To build up the church in every age until Christ returns
Scripture shows both purposes, and I am slow to declare either one finished

questions.q: Why do apostolic-scale miracles seem rarer today?

options.label: Because the sign gifts served the founding era and ceased with it
They are less rare than the Western church assumes, and expectation shapes what we see
I do not know, and I would rather admit that than force a theory

questions.q: When someone says God gave them a word for you, your first instinct is to...

options.label: Test it against Scripture, which is where God has promised to speak
Listen and weigh it carefully, since the New Testament tells churches to do exactly that
Take it seriously and slowly, assuming neither fraud nor revelation

questions.q: How do you read the promise that tongues will cease in 1 Corinthians 13?

options.label: The partial ceased when the completed witness of Scripture arrived
The partial ceases when the perfect comes, and the perfect is seeing Christ face to face
The passage is about love outlasting every gift, and I hesitate to build a timetable on it

questions.q: If you must risk an error, which risk do you choose?

options.label: Restraint, because counterfeit gifts have wounded real churches
Expectation, because quenching the Spirit is also a sin Scripture names
Neither, so I keep both warnings on the table and move slowly

questions.q: What do you make of praying for healing today?

options.label: God heals today in answer to prayer, but the sign gift of healing belonged to the apostolic era
God still gives gifts of healing to his church, and we should ask boldly
I pray for healing gladly and leave the mechanism entirely in God's hands

questions.q: Reports of miracles from the global church make you think...

options.label: God works everywhere in providence, and frontier missions may see unusual works, but the normative gifts ended
This is exactly what the New Testament would lead me to expect
Some are surely true and some surely are not, and each deserves honest testing

questions.q: Which sentence is closest to your heart?

options.label: God speaks today through the finished word, and it is enough
Earnestly desire the gifts, and test everything, both commands still standing
I will not forbid what Scripture does not forbid, or chase what it does not promise

results.name: Leaning Cessationist
results.blurb: You tend to believe the miraculous sign gifts confirmed the apostles and the giving of Scripture, completed that work, and ceased with the apostolic age. This view guards the finality and sufficiency of the written word and protects churches from manufactured wonders. Many find here a deep quiet confidence that God still heals and guides, through means he has already given.

results.name: Leaning Continuationist
results.blurb: You tend to believe all the gifts continue until Christ returns, since the New Testament never announces their retirement, and that churches should desire them earnestly and test them carefully. This view takes both of Paul's commands at full weight. Many believers around the world find here an expectancy that matches the book of Acts they read.

results.name: Leaning Open but Cautious
results.blurb: You tend to hold that Scripture never clearly ends the gifts, so you stay open, while the documented abuses keep you sober and slow. This view refuses to forbid what the Bible does not forbid or to chase what it does not promise. Many pastors and thoughtful believers live here, testing everything and holding fast to what is good.
